why_there_is_no_record: Built, and deliberately not measured. This is the first packaging run in this repository that succeeded on a version string carrying a pre-release suffix: the linux, windows and macos jobs all came back green and the run uploaded one artifact per platform. That is a build result, not a measurement. A release candidate is a rehearsal -- what it has to prove is that the pipeline can produce a binary from this version string, and 2.0.0rc1.json already records a tag that proved the opposite for its own. No sweep was run at this tag: benchmarks/perf_baseline.py and benchmarks/compare/run_comparison.py were not executed, so there is no run to point at and no figure to record.
how_this_differs_from_2_0_0rc1: Both entries are recorded: false, and the two absences are not the same absence, so this file says which one it is rather than letting a reader infer it. rc1's build died on all three platforms and produced no artifact at all, so there was nothing that could have been measured even in principle -- any figure in that file would have described a binary that does not exist. rc2's build succeeded and produced three artifacts, and the measurement was simply never taken, because a rehearsal is not a measurement point and running a sweep at a tag nobody installs would put a number in this directory that describes a commit rather than a release.
the_evidence_for_the_build_is_the_tag_bu: The v2.0.0rc2 tag has since been cut, and its own build is the evidence: linux, windows and macos all success and three artifacts uploaded (140,050,466 / 365,586,230 / 432,048,957 bytes), so the pipeline can produce a binary from this version string on every platform. The build job is not the whole run, though, and this entry must not read as though it were. The release job -- the one that assembles the archives, writes the SBOM, hashes what ships and creates the Release page -- failed: it runs tools/release_checksums.py, which imports yaml, and the job was never given that dependency. It declares an interpreter and nothing else. So the tag produced artifacts that can be downloaded from the run, and no GitHub Release page, because the job that creates one died on ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml'. That defect is repaired after this tag (the release job now installs pyyaml, and tools/ci_selfcheck.py deps guards it on every pull request), which is what 2.0.0rc3.json rehearses. When this entry was first written only a workflow_dispatch run 37055053155 on main existed and the tag had not yet been cut; both of those sentences are now false and have been replaced by this one.
what_this_tag_actually_proves: Two things, neither of them a benchmark. First, that the pipeline can build a pre-release version string at all -- which is the question 2.0.0rc1.json could only answer in the negative. Second, that the repair which came after rc1 holds on a real packaging run and not merely inside the guard: e45ecbf pointed packaging/gigaxml.spec at the same tools.make_version_info.version_quad the installer asks, and added tools/spec_check.py, which executes the spec on every pull request. Both were in this tree. A green build is not evidence that the reduction is right for every shape -- that is what the guard is for -- but it is evidence the fix is not load-bearing on luck.
no_numbers_were_fabricated_here: Deliberately empty of numbers, and for a different reason than the entry before it. This is the one place in this directory where the risk is real: the run did produce artifacts, and an artifact has a size. gigaxml-gui-windows, gigaxml-gui-linux and gigaxml-gui-macos were uploaded, and their byte counts are the size of a PyInstaller bundle -- what got shipped, not how fast anything parsed a document. They are not recorded here because recording them would put a figure in this file that reads like a performance measurement and is not one. The three names are given because they are the evidence that the build succeeded; what would be wrong is the next instinct, which is to quote their sizes next to a version number and let the reader do the rest.
what_would_close_this: The 2.0.0 release, for the same reason 1.2.1.json gives. A release candidate is cut to rehearse the pipeline, and rehearsing is what this tag was for; the figures that belong in this directory are the ones taken at a version somebody installs. perf_baseline.py and run_comparison.py now write schema_version, an identity block, the generated dataset's seed and digest, and every individual run's raw values, so the 2.0.0 record will be generated rather than reconstructed. Until then 2.0.0rc2's performance is unknown -- not equal to 2.0.0rc1's, which also has no record, and not equal to 1.1.0's, which has one taken six commits past its own tag.
